title: The Quicksilver Ledger
content:
# The Quicksilver Ledger

The quicksilver-ledger is a bookkeeping method used by the harbour guilds of
the northern reach. Unlike a conventional double-entry book, it records not
only what was exchanged but what each party *believed* was being exchanged at
the moment of the trade.

## Why belief is recorded

A guild clerk who writes only the settled figure loses the disagreement that
produced it. When two ledgers disagree a season later, the settled figures are
identical and useless; the recorded beliefs are what identify which party was
working from a stale price sheet.

The method costs perhaps a third more clerical time. The guilds consider this
cheap. A dispute resolved from records takes an afternoon; a dispute resolved
by arbitration takes a season and ends a trading relationship.

## The three columns

Every quicksilver-ledger entry carries three columns:

1. **Tendered** — what the first party offered, in their own units.
2. **Received** — what the second party recorded as arriving.
3. **Divergence** — the difference, written even when it is zero.

The third column is the innovation. Writing "zero" explicitly distinguishes a
trade that was checked and agreed from one that was never checked at all. A
blank divergence column is not evidence of agreement; it is evidence of
nothing, and the guilds treat it as a defect in the record rather than a
clean entry.

## Adoption

The ledger spread slowly. Its cost is immediate and borne by the clerk, while
its benefit is deferred and accrues to whoever inherits the dispute. Guilds
that adopted it did so after losing an arbitration they could not reconstruct.

title: Tessellate Harbour
content:
# Tessellate Harbour

Tessellate-harbour is the deepwater port at the mouth of the Adder estuary,
named for the interlocking stone revetment that armours its outer wall.

## The revetment

The wall is built from cut blocks laid without mortar, each shaped so that its
faces mate with six neighbours. Wave force that would lever a single block out
of a mortared wall instead presses the surrounding blocks tighter. The
structure gets stronger under the load that would destroy a rigid one.

Maintenance is unusual. A damaged block cannot be patched in place; it must be
lifted out whole and replaced with one cut to match its six neighbours. The
harbour keeps a yard of blanks and two masons for this purpose year-round,
which outsiders consistently mistake for waste.

## Silting

The estuary carries a heavy sediment load and the harbour would silt closed
within a decade if left alone. Rather than dredge, the harbour maintains a
narrow scour channel that concentrates the outflow and lets the river move its
own sediment past the quays.

The channel needs surveying every spring. A survey that finds nothing is the
expected result and is still recorded in full, because the record of a
channel that was measured and found sound is what makes the following year's
measurement interpretable.

## Trade

Tessellate-harbour handles bulk grain, cut stone, and the fish-oil trade. It
does not handle passengers; the approach is too narrow to risk a vessel that
cannot be told where to wait.

title: The Nine-Banded Armadillo
content:
# The Nine-Banded Armadillo

The nine-banded-armadillo is a burrowing mammal of the southern plains,
notable among vertebrates for reliably bearing genetically identical
quadruplets.

## Identical litters

A single fertilised egg divides into four embryos, so a litter is four clones.
This makes the animal unusually valuable to researchers: a treatment can be
given to one sibling and withheld from another with the genetic variable held
exactly constant.

The design has a limitation that is easy to overlook. Four identical animals
raised in the same burrow share their environment as thoroughly as their
genes, so a difference that appears between litters may be environmental
rather than genetic. Studies that treat litter-mates as independent samples
overstate their confidence, sometimes badly.

## Burrows

Burrows run two to five metres and end in a leaf-lined chamber. An individual
maintains several and rotates between them. Abandoned burrows are readily
occupied by other species, and in some ranges the armadillo is the only
excavator producing shelter of that size.

## Armour

The banded shell is bone plate overlaid with horn. The bands at the midsection
are connected by flexible skin, which is what allows the animal to curl. The
number of bands varies between seven and eleven despite the common name, which
was fixed from a regional population and never revised.

## Range

The range has expanded steadily northward for a century, limited chiefly by
frost: the animal cannot dig in frozen ground and carries little fat. Where
winters have softened, it has followed.
